Add fractions by matching the pieces

Put thirds with thirds, then see how equivalent fractions let halves and quarters work together.

Count pieces of one size

You have two eighths of a paper strip and receive three more eighths. All the pieces match, so you now have five eighths: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8.

The denominator stays eight because the pieces are still eighths. It does not become sixteen just because two groups were combined. You are counting more pieces of the same size.

Try it yourself

Choose the number of equal pieces in a whole, then choose how many pieces each pile contributes. The strips show the two amounts and their combined total.

Try three quarters plus two quarters. Five quarter-pieces make one whole and one extra quarter: 5/4 = 1 1/4. A fraction can be larger than one; the numerator is allowed to exceed the denominator.

+

Try it yourself

Bring the pieces together

Keep the pieces the same size as you add. The total may exceed one whole.

Match sizes before adding

One half and one quarter are not the same kind of piece. Rename the half as two quarters. Then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. The answer is three quarters, not two sixths.

For one third plus one sixth, turn the third into two sixths. Now 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6, which is one half. Equivalent fractions let you count matching pieces.

Check whether the answer makes sense

Adding two positive fractions gives a result larger than either starting amount. If your answer to one half plus one quarter is smaller than a half, stop and check the pieces.

Before the quiz, explain an example aloud: “These are eighths. I have two, then three more, making five eighths.” Naming the pieces keeps the denominator’s job clear. You now have the foundations for percentages and recipe measurements.
